vignette:
Moana Tui is a 63-year-old married American woman of Oceanian background who works as a project manager for a commercial construction firm. She came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle things on her own, only to find that medical reminders were shaping more and more of her days. The illness that nearly killed her began abruptly last year, when what she had taken for an ordinary period of fatigue and discomfort escalated into a medical emergency. She remembers the hospital in fragments that are not really fragments at all, but total sensory returns: the sharp chemical smell, the glare of overhead lights, the cold rail at her side, the sight of tubing and needles entering her body, and the fixed position she had to lie in while staff moved quickly around her. At the time, she understood she might die. What has stayed with her most powerfully is not a neat story she can tell from beginning to end, but the felt immediacy of being trapped in a failing body while strangers handled it.

When Moana tries to describe that period, her words often stop short. She says she "can't get it out right," then falls silent, pressing her arms stiffly against her sides as though she is back on the hospital bed. In session, when the memory comes close, her body seems to remember before language does. She becomes rigid and still in the same position she recalls from examinations and procedures, and she says it suddenly feels as if she is there again, not remembering but reliving it fully. The sensations come back all at once-the pressure, the exposure, the panic, the sense of her body no longer belonging to her. For Moana, what happened is difficult to place into ordinary speech; it arrives as a total experience rather than a narrative.

Since recovering medically, she has not felt restored to the person she was. She had once relied on herself as steady, capable, and physically durable, someone who kept complicated projects moving and handled pressure without much fuss. Now she has come to believe that her body cannot be trusted. Minor physical sensations can make her uneasy, not because she reports new symptoms, but because the earlier collapse convinced her that her body can betray her without warning. Alongside that fear is a deep shame about what happened to her body during the illness and treatment. She speaks about it with lowered eyes, as if the vulnerability of being examined, punctured, and managed by machines marked her in a way other people might somehow see. At her bleakest, she says it feels as though her life has been destroyed by what happened, as if everything after the illness has been organized around its shadow.

This shows up repeatedly in her daily life. At work, Moana spends much of her time in meetings, and she has found that certain conversation topics can abruptly change the room for her. A casual discussion of a colleague's surgery, someone mentioning an IV in the hospital, or even routine talk about an aging parent's tests can make her attention vanish. She stops following the spreadsheet on the screen or loses the thread of the construction timeline she is supposed to be leading. Sometimes she becomes curt or visibly irritable, cutting people off more sharply than she intends. She knows coworkers have noticed that she is less patient than she used to be. She hates that version of herself, but in the moment she feels keyed up and cornered.

Medical settings are especially difficult. The sight of needles, drips, or examination equipment is enough to make her body tense before she has fully registered why. During follow-up medical appointments, she braces herself on the exam table and feels dread rising the moment a clinician prepares to examine her. If a nurse or doctor touches her unexpectedly, she startles intensely, as if her body reacts before her mind catches up. At home, this has spilled into her marriage as well. If her husband reaches for her suddenly when she is distracted, she can jerk in alarm and then feel embarrassed and angry, not at him exactly, but at how quickly her body flips into alarm.

Over the months, these reactions have narrowed her world. She has not stopped working, but she prepares obsessively before any health-related appointment and dreads even conversations that might drift toward illness. The immediate problem that brought her in was a recent medical examination after which she went back to her car shaken, unable for several minutes to remember why she had come to that part of town. That frightened her almost as much as the appointment itself. Sitting in therapy now, Moana says what she fears most is that she will never feel at home in her own body again, that every reminder will keep bringing her back to that bed. What she hopes for, quietly and with some hesitation, is to be able to hear, see, or undergo ordinary medical care without feeling as though her life is being swallowed all over again.
